Well, that's... that's a tricky question, because I guess I don't really know anymore? Like, I used to play a lot of video games back in high school and my first year of college, and I remember actually getting excited about them. Like, that's what a normal 22-year-old does. But when I'm there, I'm just kind of... there. It's like there's this invisible glass wall between me and the fun everyone else is having. I can see it, I know I'm supposed to be experiencing it, but it just doesn't reach me. So I guess, no, I don't really find pleasure in much of anything lately. It all just feels like going through the motions, you know? Just... doing the things because they're on the schedule, not because they actually make me feel good.

Ending my life? Um... no. No, I haven't. I mean, I know that's a really common thing when people feel down for a long time, but for me, it's... it's not really like that? Like, if there was a button I could push to just pause everything—just go to sleep for a month or a year and not have to carry this weight around, not have to wake up and do the commute and log into the analytics software and pretend to be a functioning person—I would absolutely push that pause button. 

But actually ending my life? No. I wouldn't do that to my parents, for one thing. Especially my mom, she's so invested in me doing well right now, and the thought of putting her through that is just... no. And honestly, I don't even have the energy for something like that anyway. It's just this passive exhaustion. I just want the heavy, gray feeling to go away, I don't want *me* to go away, if that makes sense. I just keep waking up and doing the routine, day in and day out, hoping eventually the fog lifts. So, no, I've never actually thought about ending it. It's just a really long, boring, gray movie that I feel stuck watching, but I'm not trying to walk out of the theater.

Worse in the morning? Um... let me think about how to answer that. I mean, mornings are definitely hard, but I wouldn't say I feel *significantly worse*, if that makes sense. Like, when my alarm goes off at 6:30, I really, really don't want to get out of bed. I usually hit snooze three or four times, just lying there staring at the ceiling, completely dreading the whole process of having to shower and make coffee and get on the train for my commute. But the actual heavy feeling itself? It's not actually worse or more intense then. It's exactly the same as it is at 2 PM when I'm staring at a data set, or at 8 PM when I'm sitting in my apartment. 

It's just that in the morning, I have the whole day stretching out in front of me, so the prospect of having to carry that lead vest around for another sixteen hours is just... exhausting to think about. But the weight of the vest doesn't change. Like I was saying before about trying to track the variables in my day? I actually looked for a time-of-day pattern. I thought maybe I was just struggling with mornings, or maybe I needed to adjust my caffeine intake, so I mentally tracked how I felt at 9 AM versus 3 PM versus the evening. And the line on that mental graph is just completely flat. There are no morning spikes. It's just a steady, unbroken gray line from the second I open my eyes to the second I close them. So, no, it doesn't hit me harder in the morning. It's just already there, waiting for me the exact second I wake up, exactly the same as it was when I went to sleep.

Moving more slowly... um, no, actually. I really don't think so. It's funny you ask that, because I know exactly what you mean—like in movies where someone is feeling down and they're literally walking in slow motion, or just staring blankly at the wall with one shoe on for twenty minutes before they leave the house. But for me, the actual physical mechanics of my day haven't slowed down at all. 

Like, I'm a management analyst, right? So my whole job revolves around efficiency and timelines and processing information. And if I were actually moving slower, or if tasks were taking me longer, I would definitely have noticed a drop in my metrics. I would be missing deadlines. But I still get my reports done in the exact same timeframes. I still type at the exact same speed. If you looked at my project logs, there's no evidence of me taking three hours to do a one-hour task. 

And it's the same with my daily routine. Even in the morning—like I said before, I hit snooze and I dread getting up, but once my feet actually hit the floor, it still takes me exactly twenty-two minutes to shower, get dressed, and get out the door. And my walk to the train is exactly fourteen minutes, same as it always is. I'm not dragging my feet on the pavement or physically lagging behind other commuters on the sidewalk. 

So externally, my output speed is exactly the same. It's just the *internal* experience of doing it that feels different. It's like... okay, imagine you're driving a car, and you're still going exactly sixty miles per hour, so you're getting to your destination at the exact same time.
